summary: Defines how to use the X.500 Directory to help map between X.400 O/R addresses and RFC 822 mailboxes. It is experimental and was replaced by RFC 2164.

plainLanguage.summary: A translator list for two kinds of email addresses kept in a big directory.

questions: how to map x.400 addresses to rfc 822
x.500 directory for mail address mapping
how does x.400 differ from rfc 822 email
how do mail gateways translate addresses
subtitle: Using X.500 Directory to map between two email address systems.

tldr.problem: Two email systems existed in the early Internet: X.400 (from telephone standards organizations) and RFC 822 (Internet email). Mail gateways needed a reliable, distributed way to translate addresses between these incompatible systems.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 1838 defines how to store mapping information in the X.500 Directory Service. It creates two subtrees to represent X.400-to-RFC 822 mappings and the reverse, using object classes and attributes that point between the two address hierarchies.
tldr.outcome: This provided a scalable, distributed approach to maintaining address mappings instead of using centralized tables. It was experimental and later replaced by RFC 2164 as the email world consolidated around Internet standards.

today: RFC 1838 is experimental and was obsoleted by RFC 2164. It represents an effort to bridge X.400 and RFC 822 email systems during the transition period when both coexisted. Today, RFC 822 derivatives (SMTP) have become the universal email standard, and X.400 is largely obsolete.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 1838 defines how to use the X.500 Directory to support mapping between X.400 O/R (Originator/Recipient) Addresses and RFC 822 email mailboxes. This addresses a practical problem in the early 1990s: two incompatible email systems coexisted on the Internet, and mail gateways needed a way to translate addresses between them.

RFC 1327 had already defined the translation algorithm; this RFC specifies how to store and distribute the mapping information within the X.500 Directory Service rather than in static tables. This approach enables distributed management and replication of the mapping data, making it more scalable than centralized table-based approaches.
sections.plainLanguage: This document explains how to store translator lists for two email systems in a directory so mail gateways can look up addresses.

sections.title: X.400 and RFC 822 Addresses
sections.content:
X.400 uses O/R Addresses structured as a hierarchy of attributes such as Country (C), Administration Management Domain (ADMD), Private Management Domain (PRMD), and Organization (O). For example: P=UK.AC; A=Gold 400; C=GB.

RFC 822 email addresses use a simple domain-based format: user@example.com. The two systems are fundamentally incompatible: X.400 addresses are deeply hierarchical while RFC 822 addresses are flat domains. RFC 1838 shows how to represent both hierarchies in the X.500 Directory Information Tree (DIT) as separate subtrees, enabling each to be indexed and looked up for translation to the other.
sections.plainLanguage: X.400 addresses are like postal addresses with country, city, and organization. RFC 822 addresses are simple like name at domain.com. The directory stores both so mail can travel between them.

sections.title: Mapping Structure in the Directory
sections.content:
The RFC establishes two subtrees under OU=X.400/RFC 822 Mapping, O=Internet: one for X.400-to-RFC 822 mappings and one for the reverse direction. The X.400-to-RFC 822 subtree is organized under an O/R Address hierarchy, while the RFC 822-to-X.400 subtree uses a domain component hierarchy.

Two new object classes are defined: rFC822ToX400Mapping and x400ToRFC822Mapping. Attributes like associatedORAddress, associatedDomain, and associatedX400Gateway hold the actual mapping values, creating pointers between the address systems. This structure allows both distributed management and efficient lookup using the directory's search capabilities.
sections.plainLanguage: The directory has two filing cabinets: one for X.400-to-email translations and one for email-to-X.400. Each entry is a record that points from one address type to the other.

sections.title: Address Lookup Process
sections.content:
When translating an X.400 address like P=UK.AC; A=Gold 400; C=GB, a gateway derives a directory name from the address components and looks it up in the X.400-to-RFC 822 subtree. If an exact match is not found, the directory lookup indicates the longest match, which is then looked up to find the mapped domain.

The reverse process for RFC 822-to-X.400 translation is analogous: derive a directory name from the domain part (e.g., AC.UK becomes DomainComponent=AC, DomainComponent=UK), look it up in the RFC 822-to-X.400 subtree, and retrieve the associated O/R Address or gateway address. The RFC notes that translations can always be accomplished with at most two lookups, making the approach efficient even for complex hierarchies.
sections.plainLanguage: To translate an address, the gateway asks the directory for the closest match, then uses that to find the full translation.

sections.title: Advantages of Directory-Based Mapping
sections.content:
Using the X.500 Directory for mappings offers several advantages over static tables. The mapping information can be widely replicated and accessed with the directory's standard protocols, avoiding the need for a single centralized authority or service. Different organizations can manage their own mappings in the namespace they control, supporting distributed administration.

The directory structure naturally handles partial or omitted address components (e.g., when only the country and ADMD are specified). Because mappings are stored as attributes in the DIT, aliases can be used to simplify some table mappings, and numeric country codes can be supported as an alternative to textual names.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of one big table, the directory spreads the translation lists across many computers that can share and update them.
